v.q: What are the three phases of a Gradle build, in order?
o: Initialization, configuration, execution
Configuration, initialization, execution
Compilation, testing, packaging
Resolution, execution, publication
v.w: Initialization picks the projects, configuration builds the task graph without running tasks, and execution runs the requested tasks.

v.q: Which phase of a Gradle build decides which projects take part?
o: Initialization
Configuration
Execution
Publication
v.w: Initialization reads settings.gradle and picks the projects. Configuration builds the task graph and execution runs the tasks.

v.q: A task shows UP-TO-DATE in the output. What does that mean?
o: Its inputs and outputs match the last run, so Gradle skipped the work
It was loaded from a remote cache on a shared server
It could not run because it has no source files
It finished successfully and has just been executed
v.w: Gradle compares fingerprints of inputs and outputs. FROM-CACHE means restored from the cache, and NO-SOURCE means there was nothing to process.

v.q: A task shows FROM-CACHE. What happened?
o: Its output was restored from the build cache
It was skipped because it had no source
It ran and produced a new output
It failed and was retried
v.w: FROM-CACHE means a previous result was reused. UP-TO-DATE means local inputs and outputs were unchanged.

v.q: Which dependency configuration should you use for a library whose types appear in your module's public method signatures?
o: api
implementation
runtimeOnly
compileOnly
v.w: api exposes the dependency to modules that compile against yours. With implementation, consumers cannot see its types and fail to compile.

v.q: Which configuration is NOT right for a library type used in your public API?
o: implementation
api
java-library with api
api for exposed types only
v.w: implementation hides the dependency from consumers, so their compile classpath misses the types.

v.q: What is the main benefit of using implementation instead of api?
o: A change in the library does not force dependent modules to recompile
The library is excluded from the runtime classpath of the application
The library is downloaded only when a test needs it
The dependency version is chosen by the highest version rule
v.w: implementation keeps the dependency off consumers' compile classpath, so fewer modules are recompiled, and the classpath stays small.

v.q: Which statement about implementation versus api is NOT true?
o: implementation makes consumers recompile on every change
implementation keeps types off the consumer compile classpath
api exposes the dependency to consumers
implementation can speed up builds
v.w: Hiding the dependency is exactly what avoids unnecessary recompilation.

v.q: Two libraries need different versions of Jackson. Which does Gradle choose by default?
o: The highest version requested anywhere in the graph
The version nearest to the root project
The version declared first in the build file
None, and the build fails until you choose one
v.w: Gradle picks the highest version, unlike Maven's nearest definition. dependencyInsight shows why a version was selected.

v.q: Gradle finds Jackson 2.14 and 2.17 in the graph. Which statement is NOT true?
o: It always picks the version nearest the root
It picks the highest version by default
A constraint or strict version can override it
dependencyInsight shows why a version was chosen
v.w: Maven uses nearest wins. Gradle picks the highest version unless told otherwise.

v.q: Why should a build script avoid doing real work directly at the top level?
o: Top-level code runs in the configuration phase on every build
Top-level code is ignored unless a task is run explicitly
Top-level code runs only after all tasks have finished
Top-level code cannot read files from the project directory
v.w: Configuration runs on every invocation, so slow code there delays all builds and breaks the configuration cache. Do work in task actions.

v.q: Which code belongs inside a task action, not at the top of a build script?
o: Calling a REST API to fetch data
Applying a plugin
Declaring dependencies
Setting the group name
v.w: Top-level code runs on every build during configuration. Real work should happen only when the task runs.

v.q: How does the build cache differ from the up-to-date check?
o: It reuses outputs from any earlier run, including other machines or CI
It only works while the Gradle daemon is running in memory
It compares the new build with the previous run of the same task only
It stores downloaded dependency jars outside the project
v.w: The build cache is keyed by an input hash and can be shared remotely. The up-to-date check only looks at the last run in the same workspace.

v.q: Which statement about the Gradle build cache is NOT true?
o: It only reuses results from the previous run on the same machine
A remote cache can share results across CI and developers
Cached outputs are keyed by the inputs
A task can be FROM-CACHE
v.w: Unlike the up-to-date check, the build cache can reuse outputs from any earlier run, including other machines.

v.q: How should shared build logic be organised in a large multi-project build?
o: In convention plugins that each project applies
In allprojects blocks copied into every build file
In a single build file that lists every task by hand
In environment variables read by each project
v.w: Convention plugins in build-logic or buildSrc keep configuration in one place, are easier to cache and read than allprojects and subprojects blocks.

v.q: Which structure shares logic across subprojects without copying it?
o: A convention plugin
Pasting allprojects into every file
An environment variable
A long root script of tasks
v.w: A convention plugin packages common configuration, and each project applies it by id.
